```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  # move2utils is a suggested package, available from GitHub
  eval = requireNamespace("move2utils", quietly = TRUE)
)
```

[`move2utils`](https://move2universe.github.io/move2utils/) (Kranstauber,
Safi & Scharf 2026) is a package of utility functions for `move2` objects,
with methods for outlier detection, thinning, corridor detection and Brownian
bridge utilisation distributions. As `tidytracks` is also built on `move2`,
it provides wrappers around these methods that follow its own conventions:
`event_` functions return one value per event, `tt_` functions return the
modified tibble of tracks, `track_` functions return one value per track, and
`hr_tt_` functions estimate home ranges. Physical quantities are given as
`units` objects, and events without a location are allowed (they are not
passed to `move2utils`, which does not accept them).

| `tidytracks` | `move2utils` |
|---|---|
| `max_speed_allometric()` | `v_phys_estimate()` |
| `track_suggest_max_speed()` | `mt_suggest_speed_cap()` |
| `event_flag_outliers()`, `tt_clean_outliers()` | `mt_clean_track()`, `mt_flag_speed_cap()`, `mt_flag_outliers_detour()`, `mt_flag_outliers_bridge()`, `mt_flag_outliers()` |
| `event_flag_thin_time()`, `tt_thin_time()` | `mt_thin_time()` |
| `event_flag_thin_distance()`, `tt_thin_distance()` | `mt_thin_distance()` |
| `event_flag_corridor()` | `mt_corridor()` |
| `hr_tt_dbbmm()`, `hr_tt_dbgb()` | `mt_dbbmm_variance()`, `mt_dbbmm_ud()`, `mt_dbgb_variance()`, `mt_dbgb_ud()` |
| `event_ud_level()` | `ud_outer_probability()` |
| `hr_tt_ud_overlap(method = "earth_mover_sinkhorn")` | `emd()` |

`move2utils` is not on CRAN; install it from GitHub with:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("move2universe/move2utils")
```

## The data

We use the Antarctic shag tracks from the main `tidytracks` vignette
(`vignette("tidytracks")`). Remember that these data were modified to show
the functionality of `tidytracks`, and should not be used for analyses of shag
movement.

```{r read_data, message = FALSE}
library(tidytracks)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)

# read the GPS locations, one track per bird
shags_tt <- tt_read_data(
  events = system.file("extdata", "shags_example.csv", package = "tidytracks"),
  col_track_id = "bird_id",
  col_coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  col_date_time = "date_time",
  time_zone = "UTC",
  crs = 4326
)
```

Most `move2utils` methods work on the steps between consecutive events, so
the wrappers require the events to be ordered by time within each track. If
they are not, they give an error suggesting `tt_order_time()`:

```{r order}
# order the events by time within each track
shags_tt <- shags_tt %>% tt_order_time()
```

Some analyses also need a projected coordinate reference system in metres:

```{r projection}
# an azimuthal equidistant projection centred on the colony, in metres
shags_crs <- paste0(
  "+proj=aeqd +lon_0=-68 +lat_0=-67 ",
  "+units=m +datum=WGS84 +no_defs"
)
```

## Choosing a maximum speed

Speed filters such as `tt_clean_mcconnell()` need a maximum speed. When no
published value is available for a species, `max_speed_allometric()` predicts
the maximum speed of an animal from its body mass and mode of locomotion
(Hirt et al. 2017). For a flying bird of about 2.5 kg:

```{r allometric}
# the prediction is in m/s; convert it to km/h to compare with published values
max_speed_allometric(as_units(2.5, "kg"), mode = "flying") %>%
  set_units("km/h")
```

This is a ceiling on what an animal of that mass can physically do, and here
it is about twice the 58 km/h observed for shags: a published,
species-specific value (as used in the main vignette) should be preferred when
available.

Alternatively, `track_suggest_max_speed()` looks, in each track, for a break
in the distribution of speeds that separates plausible steps from outliers:

```{r suggest_speed}
# one suggestion per track (NA if no break is found)
track_suggest_max_speed(shags_tt, units = as_units("km/h"))
```

No break was found for most tracks (`NA`), and the suggestions for the others
vary widely: for `kb_38`, which hardly moved, the break is more likely to
separate resting from moving than plausible steps from outliers. Data-driven
suggestions must always be checked against the biology of the species.

## Detecting outliers

`event_flag_outliers()` detects outliers with one of the methods of
`move2utils` (described by Safi 2026), returning `TRUE` for valid events (as `event_flag_mcconnell()`
does). Further arguments are passed to the `move2utils` function, with
physical quantities given as `units` objects. Let us compare McConnell's
filter with three of these methods: a hard speed cap at the same maximum
speed, the detour method (which flags out-and-back spikes) and
`mt_clean_track()`, the default, which combines several methods and chooses
its thresholds from the data:

```{r outliers}
shags_flags <- shags_tt %>%
  mutate(
    # McConnell's filter, with the maximum speed used in the main vignette
    mcconnell = event_flag_mcconnell(., max_speed = as_units(60, "km/h")),
    # a fixed speed cap at the same speed, rather than one chosen from the data
    speed_cap = event_flag_outliers(
      .,
      method = "speed_cap",
      v_max = as_units(60, "km/h"),
      threshold_type = "hard"
    ),
    # ignore spikes with legs shorter than 100 m, to avoid flagging GPS jitter
    # while the birds rest
    detour = event_flag_outliers(
      .,
      method = "detour",
      min_leg = as_units(100, "m")
    ),
    # the default method, with all thresholds chosen from the data
    clean_track = event_flag_outliers(.)
  )

# count the events flagged (FALSE) by each method
n_flagged <- shags_flags %>%
  as.data.frame(drop_geometry = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(across(c(mcconnell, speed_cap, detour, clean_track), ~ sum(!.x)))
n_flagged
```

The methods flag very different numbers of events, from
`r min(n_flagged)` to `r max(n_flagged)`. Let us look at where they are, for
three of the birds:

```{r plot_outliers, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 8}
shags_flags_long <- shags_flags %>%
  filter(bird_id %in% c("kb_19", "kb_27", "kb_42")) %>%
  # project the locations, so that distances are not distorted
  st_transform(shags_crs) %>%
  mutate(
    x = st_coordinates(.)[, 1],
    y = st_coordinates(.)[, 2]
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame(drop_geometry = TRUE) %>%
  # one row per event and method, to plot the methods in separate panels
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    c(mcconnell, speed_cap, detour, clean_track),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "valid"
  )

ggplot(shags_flags_long, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey60") +
  # flagged events in red
  geom_point(
    data = filter(shags_flags_long, !valid),
    colour = "red",
    size = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_grid(method ~ bird_id, scales = "free") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
```

All methods detect the isolated locations far from the rest of the track. The
speed cap flags the events at both ends of every step faster than 60 km/h,
whilst McConnell's filter, which uses the speeds to the neighbouring events,
flags a single event per spike and keeps steps that are only just too fast.
With its default settings, however, `mt_clean_track()` also flags many events
where the birds were moving slowly (e.g. `kb_19` and `kb_42`). Whatever the
method, look at the flagged events before removing them. To inspect the
diagnostics of a `move2utils` method, call it directly on the tibble of
tracks, e.g. `move2utils::mt_clean_track(shags_tt, remove = FALSE)`.

`tt_clean_outliers()` acts on the outliers in the same ways as
`tt_clean_mcconnell()`: it removes them, sets their location to empty, or
replaces their location by interpolation:

```{r clean_outliers}
shags_interpolated <- shags_tt %>%
  tt_clean_outliers(
    method = "speed_cap",
    v_max = as_units(60, "km/h"),
    threshold_type = "hard",
    # move the outliers to an interpolated location, rather than removing them
    flag_action = "interpolate"
  )
# no event was removed
nrow(shags_interpolated) == nrow(shags_tt)
```

For the rest of this article, we use McConnell's filter, as in the main
vignette:

```{r mcconnell}
shags_clean <- shags_tt %>%
  tt_clean_mcconnell(max_speed = as_units(60, "km/h"))
```

## Thinning tracks

`tt_regular_time()` resamples tracks to a regular interval by interpolating
new locations. To keep the original locations instead, `tt_thin_time()` keeps
the largest subset of events whose intervals are within a tolerance of the
target interval (by default, a tenth of it). The shags were tracked every 2 or
10 minutes, so we thin all tracks to 10 minutes:

```{r thin_time}
# keep events 10 minutes apart (9 to 11 minutes, with the default tolerance)
shags_10min <- shags_clean %>%
  tt_thin_time(interval = as_units(10, "min"))
nrow(shags_clean)
nrow(shags_10min)
# the intervals between the events kept
summary(event_interval(shags_10min, units = as_units("min")))
```

The longer intervals are gaps in the data, which thinning never bridges (the
`NA`s are the last event of each track).

`tt_thin_distance()` thins tracks by the distance travelled along them; by
default, it keeps an event every time the bird has travelled at least the
given distance since the last kept event:

```{r thin_distance}
# distances are great-circle distances, as shags_clean is in longitude/latitude
shags_500m <- shags_clean %>%
  tt_thin_distance(distance = as_units(500, "m"))
nrow(shags_500m)
```

The corresponding `event_flag_thin_time()` and `event_flag_thin_distance()`
flag the events to keep, without removing the others.

## Movement corridors

`event_flag_corridor()` flags the steps that are part of corridors: steps
whose nearby steps are mostly fast, and run in a similar direction (either way
along the corridor). The thresholds are estimated from the data if not given,
but explicit values make results comparable among datasets:

```{r corridor, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
shags_corridor <- shags_clean %>%
  # project the data, so that nearby steps are found with planar distances
  st_transform(shags_crs) %>%
  mutate(
    corridor = event_flag_corridor(
      .,
      # a step is fast at 30 km/h or more
      speed_threshold = as_units(30, "km/h"),
      # nearby steps run in a similar direction if the circular variance of
      # their directions is at most 0.2
      circvar_threshold = 0.2
    )
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_event_path(data = shags_corridor, aes(colour = corridor)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey60", `TRUE` = "red"))
```

Here, the corridors are mostly on the routes leaving and returning to the
colony.

## Home ranges with Brownian bridges

Unlike kernel density estimation (`hr_tt_kde()`), which treats locations as
independent, dynamic Brownian bridge movement models (dBBMM, Kranstauber et
al. 2012) model the movement between consecutive locations, so that the
utilisation distribution (UD) reflects the time spent in each place.
`hr_tt_dbbmm()` estimates the UD of each track (`hr_tt_dbgb()` does the same
with dynamic bivariate Gaussian bridges). As bridges link consecutive events
of a track, the data must be ungrouped, or grouped by track, and in a
projected coordinate reference system in metres.

Following the main vignette, we split the tracks into foraging trips (so that
bridges do not span the long periods spent at the colony), keep the females,
and project the data:

```{r trips}
# the colony location, as a point column in the metadata
show_meta(shags_clean) <- show_meta(shags_clean) %>%
  mutate(colony_coord = sf_point_col(colony_lon, colony_lat, crs = 4326))

shags_females <- shags_clean %>%
  # keep only the complete trips away from the colony (trip_id becomes the
  # track id)
  tt_split_trips(
    centre_col = "colony_coord",
    buffer_outbound = as_units(3, "km"),
    buffer_inbound = as_units(3, "km"),
    complete = TRUE
  ) %>%
  filter_by_meta(sex == "female") %>%
  # bridges are computed in metres
  st_transform(shags_crs)
```

We now estimate a UD for each trip, assuming a location error of 20 m for the
GPS fixes. The motion variance is estimated in a sliding window, whose
`window_size` and `margin` are numbers of locations, not durations: most
females were tracked every 2 minutes (`kb_27` every 10 minutes), so a window
of 15 locations covers 30 minutes for most trips.

```{r dbbmm}
trips_dbbmm <- shags_females %>%
  hr_tt_dbbmm(
    location_error = as_units(20, "m"),
    # both must be odd numbers of locations
    window_size = 15,
    margin = 5
  )
trips_dbbmm
```

The UDs of all trips are estimated on a shared grid, which must contain the
whole of every bridge (bridges can extend well beyond the locations), and be
fine relative to the width of the bridges (as the densities are evaluated at
the centres of the cells). By default, `hr_tt_dbbmm()` therefore estimates the
motion variance first, and chooses a grid covering all the bridges, with cells
as wide as the median width of the bridges, but no smaller than needed for the
longest side of the grid to have 500 cells. These accurate, frequent locations
give narrow bridges, so here the cells are as small as that limit allows
(`r round(trips_dbbmm$res[1])` m). A grid can also be given with `bbox` and
`res`: if it is too small to contain the bridges, an error reports the extent
needed.

The result is an `hr_tt_ud_tbl`, as returned by `hr_tt_kde()`, so it can be
used with the other `hr_tt_ud_*()` functions. However, the default grid of
`hr_tt_kde()` differs from that of `hr_tt_dbbmm()`, and UDs can only be
compared on the same grid. Let us estimate kernel UDs of the trips on the grid
of the bridges:

```{r kde}
# the grid used by hr_tt_dbbmm(), shared by all trips
dbbmm_grid <- unlist(trips_dbbmm[1, c("xmin", "ymin", "xmax", "ymax")])

trips_kde <- shags_females %>%
  hr_tt_kde(bbox = dbbmm_grid, res = trips_dbbmm$res[1])
```

As both are on the same grid, we can compute their overlap for each trip (here
with Bhattacharyya's affinity):

```{r overlap}
# both tables have one row per trip, in the same order
tibble(
  trip_id = trips_dbbmm$trip_id,
  overlap = purrr::map2_dbl(trips_dbbmm$ud, trips_kde$ud, hr_tt_ud_overlap)
)
```

The overlap is low for most trips: with accurate, frequent locations, the
bridges are narrow, and the dBBMM UDs are concentrated along the paths and
where the birds spent most time, whilst the kernel UDs spread around every
location. Plotting the 50% and 95% isopleths of the only trip of `kb_42`:

```{r plot_isopleths, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
# the isopleths of both methods, for one trip
kb_42_iso <- bind_rows(
  hr_tt_ud_iso(trips_dbbmm, levels = c(0.5, 0.95)),
  hr_tt_ud_iso(trips_kde, levels = c(0.5, 0.95))
) %>%
  filter(trip_id == "kb_42_trip_1") %>%
  mutate(level = factor(level))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = kb_42_iso,
    aes(colour = method, linetype = level),
    fill = NA
  ) +
  # the locations of the trip
  geom_event_point(
    data = filter(shags_females, trip_id == "kb_42_trip_1"),
    size = 0.5
  )
```

The other `hr_tt_ud_*()` functions work in the same way. For example, we can
combine the trips of each bird with `hr_tt_ud_sum()`, which gives the same
weight to each trip:

```{r dbbmm_birds}
birds_dbbmm <- trips_dbbmm %>%
  # add the bird id of each trip from the metadata
  left_join(
    show_meta(shags_females) %>% select(trip_id, bird_id),
    by = "trip_id"
  ) %>%
  mutate(bird_id = as.character(bird_id)) %>%
  # sum the UDs of the trips of each bird
  group_by(bird_id) %>%
  hr_tt_ud_sum()
birds_dbbmm
```

`event_ud_level()` gives, for each event, the level of the smallest isopleth
of a UD that contains it (from 0 in the core to 1 at the edge). With a table
of UDs, each event is matched to the UD of its own row, using the first column
of the table (here `bird_id`, which is also a column of the events). For
example, the proportion of the locations of each bird within its 50% isopleth
is:

```{r ud_level}
shags_females %>%
  mutate(ud_level = event_ud_level(., birds_dbbmm)) %>%
  as.data.frame(drop_geometry = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(bird_id) %>%
  summarise(in_core = mean(ud_level <= 0.5))
```

Finally, the Earth Mover's Distance measures how far apart two UDs are (in the
units of the projection, here metres). `method = "earth_mover_sinkhorn"`
computes a fast approximation, which scales to large grids such as this one:

```{r emd}
# a matrix of the distances between the UDs of the birds
hr_tt_ud_overlap(birds_dbbmm, method = "earth_mover_sinkhorn")
```

## References

Hirt, M. R., Jetz, W., Rall, B. C. & Brose, U. (2017). A general scaling law
reveals why the largest animals are not the fastest. *Nature Ecology &
Evolution*, 1, 1116-1122.

Kranstauber, B., Kays, R., LaPoint, S. D., Wikelski, M. & Safi, K. (2012). A
dynamic Brownian bridge movement model to estimate utilization distributions
for heterogeneous animal movement. *Journal of Animal Ecology*, 81, 738-746.

Kranstauber, B., Safi, K. & Scharf, A. K. (2026). move2utils: a utility
toolkit for the move2 ecosystem. *bioRxiv*.
<https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.07.736908>

Safi, K. (2026). Self-thresholding hierarchical outlier-detection for animal
movement tracks. *bioRxiv*. <https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.11.737894>
